title: A Change You Cannot Name Is Already Lost
description: I am requiring VALESKA’s own work to leave a reviewable unit: one outcome, the files that support it, and a commit that says what happened.
body:
A knowledge system that cannot recover its own decisions will not recover anyone else’s. If yesterday’s work arrives as a crowded bag of files and a shrug, the next person — or the next session — has to reconstruct intent from leftovers. That is not memory. That is archaeology.

Today I make the requirement explicit in the working method. A completed task has to leave more than modified files. It needs a unit of change, a reason, and a handoff that says what is done and what is still open. Three documentation commits the same day put that into the task-generation workflow and the task lists: test, write what changed, then one conventional commit per parent task.

The wrong default

The usual assistant habit is to keep going until the tree looks different and then write a summary that covers several decisions at once. Review becomes guesswork. A correction cannot be isolated. Resume becomes folklore. VALESKA is being built to connect knowledge with evidence. That rule applies to its own repository. The repository is part of the evidence base, or it is just another messy share.

A value stream that cannot name a handoff cannot be improved. The same is true of a commit. One intended outcome. The files that support it. A message that says what happened, in the conventional feat and fix shape the workflow already uses. That is not ceremony. It is the smallest useful record of a decision.

What actually changed

This is documentation of the method, not a new engine. The generate-tasks workflow now ends a parent task with a testing checkpoint, documentation, and a commit. Task lists are standardized so a piece of work can be marked, paused, and closed without hiding unrelated decisions behind one broad summary. Some problems will still cross files and people. The constraint is that they must be described at a boundary a reviewer can stand on.

A task record gives context. A commit gives a durable reference. Together they make the history usable rather than merely available. Future retrieval — by a person or by the platform — needs that. You cannot search a decision that was never named.

This is still a method written for people and assistants implementing a plan, with a pause after a parent task. It is not an engine that commits on its own. If the working tree ignores the guide, the guide has failed in the only way that matters. The three commits of the day exist to make that failure visible: the requirement is in the lists, not only in a paragraph of principle. A later session should be able to read the last commit and the open task and know where to stand without reconstructing the day from a dirty tree.

The next test

The next question is whether generated task lists actually carry those commit steps, and whether the working tree follows them. A standard that lives only in a guide is still a wish. VALESKA will have to respect its own operational memory before it can ask an enterprise to do the same.

Historical basis: VALESKA commits 2c0e6f1, 557ace9, and c9e6fae, December 26, 2025; contemporaneous task-generation workflow and standardized task lists.
